summaries.headline: Blocked Website Data Reveals Rising Teen Gambling
summaries.summary: Teenage boys are arriving at school fluent in sports betting terms like over-under and parlay, and educators say interest in gambling has intensified since sports betting's 2018 legalization made it widely accessible. Data obtained by Chalkbeat from GoGuardian, which blocks restricted webpages for schools, shows attempts to access gambling, betting, and fantasy sports sites have jumped nearly 30% since 2022, rising from 13.48 to 17.4 blocks per 1,000 students, with roughly 140,000 attempts flagged monthly. States like Massachusetts are now building sports betting into financial literacy curricula, but educators like Nebraska's Matt Pierson admit the field is still playing catch-up to an app-driven habit with almost no barrier to entry.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Bets on State Money to Save Jobs
summaries.summary: The Chicago Board of Education narrowly passed a roughly $10 billion budget Thursday that reverses hundreds of staff layoffs by assuming $150 million more in state funding than CPS officials had projected, defying warnings from CEO Macquline King. The 11-7 vote, with one abstention, came after CPS pushed for quick approval to secure short-term borrowing by Sept. 2, and district officials now say they cannot guarantee financing will arrive in time for the Sept. 4 payroll. The standoff leaves Chicago schools navigating a real risk of missed payroll and credit damage in exchange for a bet that state revenue projections will prove too conservative.

summaries.headline: Pandemic-Era Teacher Exodus Still Reshaping Classrooms
summaries.summary: A Chalkbeat analysis of 21 states finds teacher turnover spiked after 2020 and hasn't fully receded, leaving districts to rebuild staff continuity years after the pandemic disrupted schools. Texas alone lost 35,000 more teachers than it would have if pre-pandemic turnover rates had held from 2020 to 2025, equivalent to nearly 10% of its current teacher workforce, with departures driven by stagnant pay, unsustainable workloads, and eroding trust from parents and administrators. The departures represent more than a staffing gap — they've stripped classrooms of the institutional knowledge and mentorship that experienced teachers pass on, a loss that shows up in student outcomes long after the exit interviews are over.

summaries.headline: Beyond Phonics: Building Students Who Love to Read
summaries.summary: Science of Reading implementation has sharpened focus on phonics and phonemic awareness, but educators warn that decoding skills alone won't create lifelong readers without genuine engagement with books. Franklin Square Union Free School District in New York rebuilt its literacy approach after finding that standard reading passages felt redundant and robotic to students, while benchmark assessments only a few times a year failed to capture real-time progress or foster teacher-student connection around reading. The district's shift toward giving teachers more autonomy to build relationships through books—supported by technology rather than replaced by it—points to a broader tension in literacy reform between standardized rigor and the harder-to-measure work of cultivating genuine reading motivation.

summaries.headline: Professional Learning Struggles to Keep Pace With AI
summaries.summary: District leaders are finding that professional learning programs built for slower-moving initiatives can't keep up with the speed of AI adoption and shifting classroom priorities. Traditional PD models—one-off workshops, annual training days—leave teachers without the ongoing support needed as tools and expectations evolve mid-year. Districts that build flexible, continuous learning structures into their PD calendars will be better positioned to help staff adapt as new technology and priorities keep arriving faster than old training cycles can absorb.

summaries.headline: CPS Drops Furlough Plan After Union Pushback
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools CEO Macquline King pulled five districtwide furlough days from her budget proposal ahead of Thursday's Board of Education vote, following pressure from board members and unions representing teachers and support staff. The district revised its revenue assumptions, raising its TIF surplus projection by $85 million to $285 million—still less than half the record amount CPS received last year—while the nearly $10 billion budget still cuts hundreds of staff positions and freezes some spending after January. King is pushing for a Thursday vote rather than waiting until the legal deadline in late August, betting that avoiding disruption now matters more than waiting for firmer city revenue figures.

summaries.headline: Mamdani Locks In Control of NYC School Board
summaries.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani appointed 13 members to New York City's Panel for Educational Policy, securing his authority over the board that decides school closures, contracts, and major policy shifts. The appointees include an environmental justice advocate, an MTA budget official, a former early childhood policy staffer from the de Blasio administration, and several current or former public school parents, alongside three holdovers from Eric Adams' appointments. The move marks a reversal from Mamdani's campaign pledge to relinquish mayoral control, and with the board already facing pressure from AI-moratorium advocates ahead of its first meeting with new members, his appointees will quickly signal how the administration plans to navigate contentious classroom technology and policy debates.

summaries.headline: NYC Loosens Preschool Curriculum Mandate for Providers
summaries.summary: New York City Education Department officials have quietly given early childhood providers the option to switch away from The Creative Curriculum, the single program Eric Adams mandated in 2023 for all publicly funded infant, toddler, 3-K, and pre-K classrooms serving roughly 140,000 children. Providers can now apply to use one of eight pre-approved alternative curricula, provided they gather parent and teacher input, though the city has not disclosed how many have applied or been approved, and all programs must still use the GOLD assessment system that educators have called the mandate's most burdensome element. The reversal, described by Bank Street College president Shael Polakow-Suransky as "a big shift," signals the Mamdani administration's willingness to unwind Adams-era top-down curriculum mandates even as it preserves the underlying data infrastructure those mandates built.

summaries.headline: Ed Tech Backlash Is Valid, But Incomplete
summaries.summary: A Hechinger Report opinion piece from an ed-tech industry insider argues that much of the current backlash against classroom technology is justified, pointing to the common scene of students silently working through tablets and reading programs while dashboards log the activity as "engagement" and "personalized learning." The author, who has spent a decade building the tools teachers and students now use, sides with parents, politicians, and the nation's largest teacher union in questioning screen time and student-facing AI, especially in elementary grades. The piece suggests the real failure isn't technology itself but how it's been deployed and measured, leaving districts to decide whether the fix is better implementation or retreat.

summaries.headline: Chicago Board Split Over Risky Budget Bet
summaries.summary: The Chicago Board of Education faces a Thursday deadline to approve a $9.96 billion budget that cuts hundreds of teaching positions while adding special education staff, with members divided over whether to bank on revenue that hasn't materialized. District officials say they need approval this week, ahead of the legal late-August deadline, to make September payroll, a crunch driven by delayed county property tax distributions that once again leave CPS and the county treasurer's office disputing whether the shortfall is $250 million or closer to $70-80 million. Some board members want to pass a leaner, balanced budget now, while others are pushing to assume additional state funding and disputed county tax revenue will come through, a bet that could leave the district scrambling again if it doesn't pay off.

summaries.headline: Coursera Bets $100M on Ng’s New AI Venture
summaries.summary: Coursera is investing $100 million in a new startup led by Andrew Ng, the company's co-founder and a prominent figure in AI-driven education. The deal signals continued consolidation of capital and influence around AI-based learning tools, with Ng's track record in scaling online education platforms likely shaping the startup's direction. For K-12 leaders already navigating a crowded AI edtech market, the investment underscores how quickly capital is flowing toward tools that could soon shape classroom instruction and teacher training.

summaries.headline: Federal Bill Targets Opt-In for Mental Health Screenings
summaries.summary: Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois) has introduced the Parents Opt-in Protection Act, a federal bill requiring written parental consent before students take part in surveys or evaluations that collect sensitive personal information. The measure responds directly to an Illinois law signed by Gov. Pritzker in 2025 that mandates annual mental health screenings for students in grades 3-12 starting in the 2027-28 school year, with an opt-out—rather than opt-in—provision for parents. The clash over consent models signals a broader fight likely to reach other statehouses as more districts build routine mental health screening into the school calendar.

summaries.headline: Indiana Districts Turn to Voters as Costs Rise
summaries.summary: A record number of Indiana school districts are asking voters to approve property tax increases this November, as Chalkbeat Indiana seeks resident input to inform its election coverage. Districts point to declining enrollment-based state revenue, rising operational costs, and last year's property tax reform, which is expected to strip millions in revenue, as the financial pressures driving these ballot requests; under state law, districts can only exceed the 1% assessed-value cap through voter-approved referendums, and this year marks the first time such requests are restricted to the November general election. As more districts lean on local taxpayers to fill funding gaps left by state policy shifts, community response to these referendums will offer an early read on how much fiscal strain households are willing to absorb on behalf of their schools.

summaries.headline: Screen Time Retreat Exposes a Motor Skills Gap
summaries.summary: Elementary teachers are increasingly reporting that students navigate touchscreens with ease but struggle to hold a pencil, form letters fluently, or write for more than a few minutes without fatigue. The rise of classroom "digital detox" efforts, driven largely by concerns over attention spans and mental fatigue, is surfacing a less-discussed casualty of heavy device use: diminished fine and gross motor development from lost tactile, hands-on experiences. Handwriting automaticity frees cognitive bandwidth for spelling, sentence construction, and idea generation, so the physical strain of an unpracticed grip isn't just a penmanship problem — it's a direct drain on the mental energy students need for literacy itself.

summaries.headline: Chronic Absenteeism Is Stalling Academic Recovery
summaries.summary: A new NWEA report finds that districts with the highest chronic absenteeism rates are lagging furthest behind in returning to pre-pandemic achievement levels, based on an analysis of MAP Growth data from 2019 to 2024 in grades 3 through 8 overlaid with attendance figures from the American Enterprise Institute. The connection between missed school days and stalled academic gains is even more pronounced in high-poverty districts, and researchers note the effect extends beyond the chronically absent students themselves to depress outcomes schoolwide. NWEA's brief argues that attendance shouldn't be treated as a separate initiative from academic recovery but built directly into it, a framing that pushes district leaders to reconsider where absenteeism sits on their priority list.

summaries.headline: Study Questions Funding-Outcomes Link in Schools
summaries.summary: A new analysis pushes back on the long-standing assumption that simply increasing school budgets translates into better student outcomes, a narrative that has shaped decades of funding lawsuits and policy debates. The research points instead to how dollars are spent — on staffing, instructional models, and program design — as the stronger predictor of academic gains, rather than the raw size of a district's budget. For superintendents and school boards fighting for every additional dollar, the findings suggest the harder conversation isn't just about getting more money, but proving what that money is actually buying in classrooms.

summaries.headline: Tucson Unified Confronts 44% Chronic Absenteeism Rate
summaries.summary: Chronic absenteeism in Tucson Unified School District has climbed to 44%, its highest mark since 2021, prompting district leaders to roll out a new intervention plan ahead of the school year. Superintendent Gabriel Trujillo outlined the effort at a back-to-school media briefing, signaling the district views the problem as urgent enough to warrant a coordinated response rather than incremental fixes. The figure places Tucson well above pre-pandemic norms and adds to a growing body of district-level data showing that attendance recovery has stalled even as other pandemic-era disruptions have eased.

summaries.headline: Robot Teacher Purchase Stalls Over Vendor Ties
summaries.summary: Salamanca City Central School District in upstate New York has paused deployment of a $60,000 humanoid classroom robot named "Sally" after parents and teachers discovered its maker, Realbotix, shares corporate ties with RealDoll through a sister company. The state teachers union publicly opposed the plan, and residents raised additional concerns about what student data the robot and its AI assistant might collect, prompting the district to seek stronger privacy agreements with the state before moving forward with no new timeline set. The episode shows how quickly ed-tech procurement decisions can unravel once vendor backgrounds face public scrutiny, and signals that districts eyeing AI and robotics tools should vet corporate ownership as closely as the technology itself.

summaries.headline: West Virginia Rolls Out First Statewide AI Curriculum
summaries.summary: West Virginia this week became the first state to introduce a statewide AI literacy and digital science framework, training educators on it during three days of professional development sessions in Charleston. The framework spans computer science, AI literacy, data reasoning, cybersecurity awareness and media literacy, aiming to give students workforce-ready digital skills while also helping teachers personalize instruction and streamline their own work. State Superintendent Michele Blatt, who testified before a U.S. House subcommittee earlier this year on balancing AI adoption with student data protection, is positioning the framework as a model other states may look to as they navigate similar policy gaps.

Until we start tackling the problem by the roots, we will find ourselves right back here every generation. We need media literacy yes, but more importantly we need political literacy.

I don’t care where one lives, what level of education one has, what social level one is, most people in this country need to get involved in politics and realize just how important politics is to their daily lives, because from now on, things are only going to get worse in politics and in the media.

The fish might rot from the head, but the tree sickens from the roots. The problem isn’t politicians, because we elect politicians, the problem is us, the voters and until we start admitting that we’ve given up on our civic duties, cause after all it’s so easy to blame politicians, we’ll get nowhere.

Right now we are watching our infrastructures go to shit, our institutions go to shit, our economy go to shit, our guardrails disappear, our protections vanish, our rights taken away, and I’m still reading folks saying “we’re not talking to the voters the right way”.

I’m sorry but WTF? Do voters have eyes and ears? Do they not live in this country and feel the effects of this administration? One can be as low information as one is, but damn it they still live inside this country, they still pump gas, get sick, buy food, the excuse of “low information” no longer holds up, no excuse holds up.

When you’re surrounded by flames and you have a bucket of water on your left and a bucket of gasoline on your right, it’s inadmissible that you’re still debating which to throw on the fire to escape.

For the folks involved at the Brunner Literacy Center, it’s about a lot more than reading and writing. They say every student who walks through Brunner’s doors brings a unique story and every tutor helps write the next chapter of that story.

For nearly 15 years, the center has been transforming lives, helping adults across the Miami Valley overcome educational barriers and achieve personal, professional and lifelong goals through free individualized instruction. The organization serves adults ages 19 and older through four core programs: English Language Learning (ELL), Adult Basic Education, GED preparation and Continuing Education.

“We believe literacy is more than reading and writing; it is the foundation for opportunity, confidence, economic mobility and civic engagement,” said CEO Myla Cardona-Jones. “Every day we meet adults who are determined to improve their lives, whether that means earning a GED, learning English, preparing for employment, helping their children with homework, or pursuing a lifelong dream. Our job is to walk alongside them and provide the support they need to succeed.”

The need for adult literacy services continues to grow throughout Montgomery County and the surrounding region. In 2025 alone, Brunner served more than 600 adults and families through its educational programs, community partnerships and literacy initiatives.

### Meet Maria

One of those students is Maria, a resident of West Dayton, who enrolled in the Center’s English Language Learning program after arriving in the United States.

“Before Brunner, I was afraid to speak English in public,” she said. “My tutor encouraged me every step of the way. Now I can communicate with my son’s teachers, speak confidently at work and feel connected to my community.”

A one-on-one tutoring model allows students to learn at their own pace while building meaningful relationships with trained volunteer tutors. Services are offered free of charge, removing financial barriers that often prevent adults from pursuing educational opportunities.

“Our volunteers are the heart of this mission,” said Cardona-Jones. “Many people assume they need teaching experience to become a tutor, but that simply isn’t true. We provide the training, resources and ongoing support. What we need most are compassionate individuals willing to invest their time in another person’s success.”

[CONTRIBUTED](https://www.daytondailynews.com/users/profile/guest9c9307cb8a3abecaa0fd530b)

As student involvement continues to increase, the organization is actively seeking volunteer tutors for all four core programs. Volunteer tutors typically commit to meeting with a student once or twice a week.

“One hour can truly change a life,” said Cardona-Jones. “Whether you’re a retired educator, working professional, college student or simply someone who wants to give back, there is a place for you in this work.”

### Here’s what they need:

- Spiral notebooks
- Composition notebooks
- Folders with pockets
- Blue and black pens
- Pencils
- Highlighters
- Dry erase markers
- Printer paper
- Sticky notes
- Index cards
- Calculators
- Adult and children’s books
- Candy
- Gift cards for student incentives such as gas cards, grocery, restaurants.

Donations may be dropped off from 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday at Brunner Literacy Center, 1995 Shiloh Springs Road, Dayton. For larger donations, please call 937-567-9600 to arrange a delivery time.

Friday morning, the joyful sounds of campers singing as they began the closing program of Camp Curious echoed across the grounds of Shrine Mont in Orkney Springs. It was a fitting welcome to a place where learning, friendship, and discovery come together.

Camp Curious is a remarkable and transformative camp. Its name captures the very heart of its mission: to inspire curiosity and ignite courage and confidence to read and write.

Shrine Mont is an Episcopal conference center in Orkney Springs, surrounded by the beauty of the Shenandoah Valley. Each summer, the Virginia Association of Teachers of English (VATE) partners with Shrine Mont to host Camp Curious, an overnight camp designed for rising third through rising sixth graders who struggle with reading and writing. Rather than focusing solely on remediation, the camp creates an environment where literacy becomes an adventure. Certified teachers and trained camp counselors work together to infuse struggling readers and writers with the joy and experiences of reading and writing.

Campers spend their days rotating through engaging reading and writing activities while also enjoying the classic experiences that make summer camp unforgettable. They swim, learn yoga, create arts and crafts, sing, practice Readers Theatre, and read under the stars in the shadow of North Mountain. Every activity is thoughtfully designed to reinforce the camp's mission: helping children discover that reading and writing can be sources of excitement, imagination, and lifelong possibility.

Beyond literacy and outdoor adventure, campers develop valuable life skills through shared experiences, teamwork, and daily interactions. They build meaningful friendships, strengthen their communication and collaboration skills, and gain confidence in forming positive relationships with their peers. Campers cultivate resilience, independence, problem-solving abilities, and healthy coping strategies that support their growth both at camp and in their everyday lives.

Thanks to the many sponsors who contributed, Camp Curious is offered at no cost to participating families. Financial barriers should never prevent a child from learning, growing, and experiencing the magic of camp. Every child deserves the opportunity to strengthen literacy skills, build confidence, make new friends, and create memories that will last long after the final songs of the closing ceremony have faded.

Benjamin Franklin said it best: "An investment in knowledge pays the best interest." Camp Curious is an investment not only in the future of each camper but also in the future of our communities. All the campers went home with a collection of books they personally selected, a renewed enthusiasm for reading, cherished memories, and the encouragement and love of a dedicated staff committed to helping them succeed.

The true measure of Camp Curious is found in the confidence gained, the curiosity that was sparked, and the joy that now shines in their hearts. Those are gifts that will continue to grow for years to come. Thank you to all who made this camp possible!

_Joanne Poplar was born and raised in Virginia and is a proud resident of Shenandoah County._

local_articles.full_content:
![](https://readthereporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Lions-International-logo-flat-feature-777x437.jpg)

Posted By: [The Reporter](https://readthereporter.com/author/the-reporter/)July 31, 2026

The Carmel Lions Club has shared its intention to participate in the “Jim Irsay 1976 Acts of Kindness Day” in two ways on Aug. 5, in celebration of Carmel’s 50th anniversary as a city.

For the first act of kindness, the Lions Club board of directors has voted to donate $1,976 to the Trinity Free Clinic for its vision program. The clinic helps to provide free vision tests and eyeglasses to those in need. The Lions Club currently processes requests from all of Carmel’s elementary schools when eyeglasses are needed for students who cannot afford them. Students who need assistance are referred to the Trinity Free Clinic’s program. These funds will go a long way in continuing this service.

The second action will be the donation of $1,976 in children’s reading books to Carmel’s elementary schools. The Lions Club received a list of requested books from the media specialists at each school targeting reading at a second-grade level. The Lions then purchased one of each book requested for each of the 11 school libraries as part of their ongoing literacy campaign.

The Carmel Lions Club is partnering, like many other organizations, with the Kiwanis Club of Carmel and the Rotary Club of Carmel in support of this special occasion. The collaborative, community-wide initiative will feature multiple service projects across the city. Volunteers from Rotary, Kiwanis, other service organizations, local businesses and non-profits will complete 1,976 acts of kindness, honoring the memory of Jim Irsay.

In addition to the Lions’ two large acts of kindness, Lions Club members will receive an email from the organization letting them know about the contributions and encouraging each of them to also do one act of kindness on Aug. 5.

This event is intended to inspire civic pride, expand community engagement, and leave a lasting, positive mark on the city of Carmel. The Jim Irsay 1976 Acts of Kindness Day has been approved by the Indianapolis Colts for Aug. 5, 2026.
